questiontext.text:
An oscillator completes one full cycle every 0.25 s.

What is its frequency, in Hz? (Enter a number only.)

generalfeedback.text:
f = 1/T = 1/(0.25 s) = 4 Hz.

Period and frequency are reciprocals. The period answers “how many seconds per cycle,” the frequency answers “how many cycles per second.” A quarter-second per cycle means four cycles per second.

feedback.text: Correct.
You gave back the period you were told — the number of seconds per cycle. Frequency asks the opposite question: how many cycles per second?
Period and frequency are reciprocals of one another. You were given seconds per cycle; the question asks for cycles per second.

questiontext.text:
A mass oscillates according to x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ), where x is measured in meters and t in seconds.

Match each quantity to its unit.

generalfeedback.text:
T → seconds (s). f → hertz (Hz). ω → radians per second (rad/s). A → meters (m). The unused option, N/m, is the unit of a spring constant.

Read them off the equation. T is a time. f counts cycles per second. ω is an angle per unit time. And A multiplies a cosine — which is just a number — so A must carry the same units as x itself.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text:
Some matches are right, but not all of them.

For the amplitude, use this: the cosine of an angle is a pure number with no units, so whatever multiplies it must carry the units of the left-hand side. For the other three, sort them into “a time,” “per time,” and “an angle per time.” One option is left over on purpose.

incorrectfeedback.text:
Work from the equation rather than from memory.

The cosine of an angle is a pure number, so whatever multiplies it must carry the units of the left-hand side — that pins down the amplitude. Then sort the remaining symbols into “a time,” “per time,” and “an angle per time.” One option is left over on purpose.

name.text: KO1-A · Where kinetic energy is largest

questiontext.text:
A mass on a spring oscillates in simple harmonic motion.

Where is its kinetic energy largest?

generalfeedback.text:
At the equilibrium position.

The total energy stays constant while kinetic and potential energy trade back and forth. At maximum displacement the spring is stretched the most and the mass has momentarily stopped, so all the energy is potential. At equilibrium the spring is unstretched, so none of the energy is potential — it is all kinetic, and the speed is greatest there.

incorrectfeedback.text: Kinetic energy tracks speed. Trace the mass through one full cycle and ask where it is moving fastest — and where it is not moving at all.

feedback.text: Correct.
At the turning points the mass has momentarily stopped. If its speed is zero there, what is its kinetic energy? That location is where the other kind of energy peaks.
The mass is moving there, but it has not finished speeding up. It keeps accelerating for as long as the restoring force still pushes it toward the center — so where does it stop gaining speed?

answer.text: Kinetic energy is constant throughout the motion

feedback.text: The total energy is constant. Kinetic energy on its own is not — the mass is briefly stationary at each turning point, so it must vary through the cycle.

name.text: KO1-B · Angular frequency of a mass–spring system

questiontext.text:
A 2.0 kg mass hangs on a spring with force constant k = 8.0 N/m.

What is the angular frequency ω of its oscillation, in rad/s? (Enter a number only.)

generalfeedback.text:
ω = √(k/m) = √(8.0 / 2.0) = √4 = 2 rad/s.

Note the pattern: a stiffer spring oscillates faster, a heavier mass oscillates slower, and the square root means quadrupling either one only doubles the effect.

feedback.text: Correct.
You have computed k/m correctly, but stopped one step early. Look again at where the square root sits in the formula for ω.
That is the ordinary frequency f, in Hz. The question asks for angular frequency, which differs from it by a factor of 2π.
You have m/k under the root, which is upside down. Which of the two belongs on top? Sanity-check it: a stiffer spring should oscillate faster.
Use ω = √(k/m): divide first, then take the square root. The numbers here were chosen to give a tidy whole-number answer, so if yours is messy, check the order of operations.

name.text: KO2-A · What the pendulum period does not depend on

questiontext.text:
For small-angle oscillations, which of the following does the period of a simple pendulum not depend on?

Select all that apply.

generalfeedback.text:
The period does not depend on the mass of the bob or the amplitude of the swing.

T = 2π√(L/g). Only two quantities appear: the length and the local free-fall acceleration. Mass is absent — a heavy bob and a light bob on equal strings keep identical time. Amplitude is absent too, as long as the swing stays small, and that is exactly the property that made pendulums useful as clocks.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text:
You have part of it, but there is more than one right answer here.

Write down T = 2π√(L/g) and check each option against it. Any listed quantity that is missing from that formula is something the period does not depend on.

incorrectfeedback.text: Write down T = 2π√(L/g) and compare each option against it, one at a time. More than one of the four is absent from that formula.

feedback.text: Correct — mass does not appear in the period formula at all.
Correct, for small angles — a wider small swing takes the same time as a narrower one.
Check whether L appears in T = 2π√(L/g). Then picture a long pendulum beside a short one — do they swing at the same rate?
Check whether g appears in T = 2π√(L/g). Then ask whether you would expect this pendulum to keep the same time on the Moon.

name.text: KO2-B · Angular frequency of a pendulum

questiontext.text:
A pendulum of length 1.0 m swings where g = 9.8 m/s².

What is its angular frequency ω, in rad/s? (Enter a number only.)

generalfeedback.text:
ω = √(g/L) = √(9.8 / 1.0) = 3.1 rad/s.

Compare with the mass–spring case, ω = √(k/m): same structure, with g/L playing the role of k/m. If you preferred to work from the period, T = 2π√(L/g) ≈ 2.0 s and then ω = 2π/T gives the same result.

feedback.text: Correct.
You found the period, in seconds, rather than the angular frequency. The two are related by a factor of 2π — check which way round it goes.
You computed g/L and stopped. One operation remains.
That is the ordinary frequency f, in Hz. Angular frequency is larger by a factor of 2π.
For a pendulum, ω = √(g/L) — note that g sits on top, the mirror image of the L/g you see inside the period formula. Divide first, then take the square root.

name.text: KO3-A · Wave speed from f and λ

questiontext.text:
A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 4.0 m.

What is its speed, in m/s? (Enter a number only.)

generalfeedback.text:
v = fλ = (50 Hz)(4.0 m) = 200 m/s.

The units are the quickest check: hertz is 1/s, so Hz × m gives m/s directly. If a combination does not come out in m/s, it is not a speed.

feedback.text: Correct.
You divided the frequency by the wavelength. Check the units of what you did: hertz is 1/s, so Hz ÷ m cannot give m/s.
You divided the wavelength by the frequency. Check the units: which combination of Hz and m actually yields m/s?
You added the two numbers, but quantities with different units cannot be added. Check what operation gives m/s from Hz and m.
A wave advances exactly one wavelength in one period. Let the units decide the operation: hertz is 1/s, so which combination with meters gives m/s?

questiontext.text: Match each wave symbol to what it measures.

generalfeedback.text:
λ → distance between successive crests. T → time for one full oscillation. A → maximum displacement from equilibrium. v → how fast the wave pattern travels. The unused option, “number of crests passing per second,” is the definition of frequency.

Sort them by what kind of quantity each one is: λ is a distance measured along the wave, T is a time measured at one place, A is a displacement measured from equilibrium, and v = λ/T combines the first two into a speed.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text:
Some matches are right, but not all of them.

Two things to note: one of the five descriptions is the definition of frequency, and frequency is not among the symbols shown — so that description goes unused. For the four that remain, ask of each symbol whether it measures a distance, a time, or a speed.

incorrectfeedback.text: Ask of each symbol: is this a distance, a time, or a speed? Note also that one of the five descriptions defines frequency, which is not among the symbols listed — so it goes unused.

answer.text: how fast the wave pattern travels
number of crests passing per second

questiontext.text:
You tighten a guitar string without changing its length.

The speed of waves on the string

generalfeedback.text:
The wave speed increases.

v = √(T/μ). Tightening raises the tension T, while the linear mass density μ depends only on the string itself and is unchanged. Since the fundamental is f₁ = v/2L and L is fixed, the pitch rises along with the speed — which is exactly what tuning a guitar does.

incorrectfeedback.text: Use v = √(T/μ) and ask which of those two quantities you actually changed, and whether it sits above or below the line. Then sanity-check the result against a real instrument.

feedback.text: Correct.

You have the right formula in mind but the wrong direction. Check whether tension sits in the numerator or the denominator of v = √(T/μ), then test it against experience: when you tighten a guitar string, does its pitch go up or down?
Wave speed on a string is set by two things: the string's own mass per unit length, and the tension. If tension made no difference, a guitar could not be tuned at all.
A tightened string still carries waves — a tuned guitar is proof. Look at v = √(T/μ) and consider which way the speed moves.

name.text: KO4-B · Second harmonic on a fixed string

questiontext.text:
A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its second harmonic.

Which of the following are true? Select all that apply.

generalfeedback.text:
Three are true: there is a node at the midpoint, the frequency is twice the fundamental, and the wavelength equals the string length. The false one is the claim about antinodes at the fixed ends.

Sketch it. The ends are clamped, so both are nodes. The second harmonic fits exactly one full wavelength between them, so λ₂ = L, which puts a third node at the midpoint and antinodes at the quarter points. Since v is fixed by the string, halving the wavelength from the fundamental's 2L doubles the frequency: f₂ = 2f₁.

correctfeedback.text: Correct — you found all three true statements.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text:
You have some of them, but not the full set.

Draw the string. Put a node at each fixed end, since a clamped point cannot move. Now fit exactly one whole wavelength between those ends and read off the rest: how many nodes appear, where do they fall, and how does the wavelength compare with the string length?

incorrectfeedback.text: Draw the string with a node at each fixed end, then fit exactly one whole wavelength between them. Everything you need can be read off that sketch. More than one statement is true.

answer.text: There is a node at the midpoint of the string

feedback.text: Correct — the second harmonic has an interior node exactly halfway along.

answer.text: Its frequency is twice the fundamental frequency

feedback.text: Correct — that is what “second harmonic” means.

answer.text: Its wavelength equals the length of the string

feedback.text: Correct — one complete wavelength fits between the fixed ends.

answer.text: There is an antinode at each fixed end

feedback.text: The ends are clamped, so they cannot move at all. What do we call a point on a standing wave whose displacement is always zero? Antinodes have to fall somewhere else.
